description.narrative: The development objective of the Ecosystem Conservation and Management Project for Sri Lanka is to improve the management of ecosystems in selected locations in Sri Lanka for conservation and community benefits. The project comprises of four components. The first component, pilot landscape planning and management will provide technical assistance, training, and capacity building to develop the guiding framework for landscape-level management planning and support the piloting of landscape planning and management in two selected landscapes comprising contiguous areas of unique ecological, cultural, and socio-economic characteristics. The second component, sustainable use of natural resources and human-elephant co-existence will support communities living adjacent to protected area (PAs) and other ecologically sensitive areas to plan for natural resource use and to develop biodiversity compatible, productive, and climate resilient livelihood activities and to scale-up successful models that address the human-elephant conflict. It consists of two sub-components: (i) sustainable use of natural resources for livelihood enhancement; and (ii) human-elephant co-existence for livelihood protection. The third component, PA management and institutional capacity will support interventions in PAs in compliance with the fauna and flora protection ordinance (FFPO) and the forest conservation ordinance (FCO); support nature based tourism development, and strengthen the institutional capacity and investment capability for conservation and management. It consists of three sub-components: (i) PA conservation and management; (ii) nature-based tourism in protected areas; and (iii) institutional capacity and investment capability of department of wildlife conservation (DWC) and forest department (FD). The fourth component, project management will finance the project management unit (PMU) and implementing agencies in project management, project monitoring and evaluation, through the provision of incremental operating funds, consulting services, transportation, equipment, and training of administrators covering range of topics, such as administration, planning, budgeting, fiduciary activities, safeguards and monitoring and reporting on project implementation.
The project development objective (PDO) is to improve the management of ecosystems in selected locations in Sri Lanka for conservation and community benefits.

title.narrative: Reduction in crop and property damages in areas of community fencing

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (166%). </strong>The indicator measures beneficiaries’ perceived reduction in damages to crops and property as a result of community fences to mitigate HEC. It relates to the pathway on <strong>reduced likelihood and severity of HEC</strong>. At completion, the Community Beneficiary Survey shows that 71 percent of beneficiaries state that their stored crops are better protected and 87 percent of beneficiaries state that their properties are better protected as a result of permanent village fences. Overall, 75 percent of beneficiaries state that damages to their livelihoods have been reduced as a result of community fencing to mitigate HEC. Data source: Community Beneficiary Survey (www.escamp.lk).</p>

title.narrative: Range level PA management plans implemented

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (100%). </strong>The indicator tracks the number of PA management plans that have been supported in their implementation as part of the project. This indicator tracks the pathway of <strong>strengthened PA management for carrying capacity and protection of wildlife and improved tourism experience</strong>. At completion, the project has supported the implementation of 11 range-level PA management plans. These include the following ranges within the protected areas and national parks of the project area: (1) Udawalwa NP, (2) Lunugamvehera NP, (3) Bundala NP, (4) Yala NP, (5) Galoya NP, (6) Sinharaja WHS, (7) Kanneliya F.R., (8) Knuckles World Heritage Site (WHS) (Kandy), (9) Knuckles WHS (Matale), (10) Hurulu Forest Reserve (FR), and (11) Weerakkodocholai FR and Wanniyagama FR (located in the same range). Activities included direct investments to enhance wildlife habitats in protected areas through assisted natural regeneration, catchment development and rehabilitation of large rainfed water tanks, construction of smaller serviced water holes, removal of invasive alien plants, and implementation of fire control measure (fire lines). Furtherore, activities aimed at enhancing protection against encroachment on PAs (demarcation and patrolling) and reducing communities’ dependency on forest resources (alternative IGAs) are equally important in improving wildlife habitats by preventing unsustainable practices and pressure on natural resources. Data sources: Project and activity records, direct observation.</p>

title.narrative: People whose assets protected as a result of HECOEX interventions

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Partially Achieved (86%). </strong>This indicator to the pathway of <strong>reduced likelihood and severity of HEC</strong>. The indicator was introduced in April 2020. The target was revised upwards in June 2020 in proportion to the expected increased number of villages and agricultural plots fenced to protect against HEC (see linked intermediate indicator 6 below). Based on the istallation of electrical fences in 31 villages, the crops and properties of 3,295 households are better protected as a result of project interventions (see Annex 9). With an average of 4.2 members per household according to the 2021 Census of Population and Housing that means that the assets - and lives - of 13,839 people are better protected at project closing. The difference of achievement between this indicator (5) and linked intermediate 6 below is explained by the relatively larger size of villages where fences were completed (average of 106 households per village) than what was estimated at appraisal (average of 35 households per village. Data source: Community Beneficiary Survey (www.escampl.lk) and 2021 Census of Population and Housing.</p>

title.narrative: Conservation status & enforcement monitoring and reporting systems

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (100%). </strong>The indicator follows the pathway of <strong>strengthened management capacity</strong> as it was defined as the number of monitoring systems developed by end of the 3rd year to track conservation status of PAs under the FD and DWC. A target of two was set to track the implementation of the Spatial Monitoring and Reporting Tool (SMART) and of the National Frest Inventory (NFI). In a first for Sri Lanka, the project introduced SMART devices in 28 wildlife PAs in 2018.  At closing, the project had distributed a total of 100 devices to DWC park officers and delivered 11 training sessions to a total of 556 participants (including repeat participants). Training on using SMART for patrolling is now included in the curriculum of the regular training programs for DWC field staff. The Director General of DG DWC has issued a circular for continuous implementation of SMART<em>. </em>The NFI was completed in<strong> </strong>April 2023, and Sri Lanka is now seeking support to undertake the next round of data collection for the NFI with 4,550 sample plots over 5 years. The updated NFI has informed the development of the LMPs and the FSMP. Data sources: expert consultation, NFI database.</p>

<p><strong>Achieved</strong> <strong>(654%).</strong> The indicator tracks training and capacity building activities aimed at strengthening skills of FD and DWC staff and related to the pathway of <strong>strengthened management capacity</strong>. The project delivered training and capacity building to 2,027 participants from the FD and DWC under Comp. 3.A and 3.C (see Annex 10 for a complete overview of training and capacity building delivered by ESCAMP). At the park level (Comp. 3.A), some FD and DWC staff have likely prticipated in more than one training session (repeat participants), where training focused on operation of SMART patrolling devices (556 DWC participants trained) and on implementation of environmental and social safeguards instruments (562 FD and DWC participant trained). At the institutional level (Comp. 3.C), 835 FD officers and 74 DWC officers received training at the SLFI in Nuwara Eliya and NWRTC in Giritale, respectively. Upon completion, successful participation was noted in individual staff files and each staff member was invited to participate in a survey to evaluate the training (linked to OI 2). Beyond this achievement, the project trained an additional 615 participants from FD and DWC and many other public departments, private sector, and CBOs in landscape planning and management for the development of the LMPs (see intermediate indicator 1). Data source: attendance lists.</p>

<p><strong>Achieved (106%). </strong>The indicator measures the number of people benefitting directly from project activities. This is not an outcome indicator per-se and is not linked to a specific pathway. The result was assessed in the final Community Beneficiry Survey based on beneficiaries of sub-components 2(a), 2(b) and 3(b). At project completion, the number of direct beneficiaries included: (i) 8,105 people involved in income-generating activities and nature-based tourism activities (see intermediate indicator 4); 6,702 people benefitting from community development activities; and (ii) 13,839 people benefitting from HEC mitigation activities (see intermediate indicator 5). Gender target was <strong>Achieved (183%). </strong>The indicator measures the proportion of drect beneficiaries that are female with a target set at 30 percent. At project completion, women account for 53 percent of project beneficiaries for component 2.a and 3.b. Data source: Community Beneficiary Survey (www.escamp.lk)</p>

title.narrative: Supportive infrastructure upgraded for long-term capacity building

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (100%). </strong>The pathway that this indicator tracks is <strong>strengthened management capacity</strong> as the project upgraded three national conservation training and research facilities to build the long-term capacity of the FD and DWC the Sri Lanka Forestry Institute in Nuwera Eliya, the SLFI Field Training Center in Inamaluwa, and the National Wildlife Research and Training Centre in Giritale. All three facilities have been completed and handed over to the MoWFRC. The new facilities: (i) have raised the capacity of the centers to accommodate a larger number of trainees and visitors under improved conditions; (ii) are built to international standards; and have strengthened the profile of SLFI and the NWRTC as leading international research and training institutes on forestry, wildlife, and environmental conservation. Data sources: project and activity records, direct observation.</p>

<p><strong>Achieved (150%). </strong>The indicator follows the pathway of <strong>strengthened management capacity</strong> and tracked the development of two long-term training programs. At completion, the project had supported the development of FD Diploma & Certificate Courses and DWC Training Programs, including revisions to the curriculum with coursework on i.e. Landscape Management Planning, SMART Patrolling and Environmental and Social Safeguards. Data sources: course curriculums.</p>

title.narrative: Villages and agriculture plots protected as a result of human-elephant co-existence activities

<p><strong>Achieved (90%). </strong>The indicator accounts for the area of PAs to benefit from investments in habitat improvement. The indicator follows the pathways of <strong>strengthened PA management for carrying capacity and protection of wildlife and improved tourism experience</strong>. The target of 350,000 (ha) is the estimated area at the time of restructuring in April 2020 (see Annex 8). However, the actual combined area of participating PAs is 315,799 ha. The difference of 34,201 ha relates to Yala NP, where only Block I and II of a total of five blocks actually participated in the project (see Project Area<strong> </strong>in Annex 9). Thus, it may be stated that the indicator target was achieved. By project closing, the project had improved wildlife habitats on an area of 315,799 hectares (see also related outcome indicator 3). Activities included direct investments to enhance wildlife habitats in protected areas through assisted natural regeneration, catchment development and rehabilitation of large rainfed water tanks, construction of smaller serviced water holes, removal of invasive alien plants, and implementation of fire control measures (fire lines). Data sources: project and activity records, direct observation</p>

title.narrative: Knowledge products on elephant management in place

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (167%). </strong>The indicator tracks the number of knowledge products on elephant management produced and is in line with the pathway on <strong>improved management capacity</strong>. At completion, the project had produced five such knowledge products. First, a DNA study to identify the genetic composition of the elephant population island-wide to inform decision-making on conservation of the elephant population, i.e. whether to translocate elephants between regions (June 2022). Second, an Elephant Collaring Programme to analyse movement and distribution patterns to identify the home range of elephants has been completed with the participation of 39 elephants. The final report is still outstanding at project closing. Third, an elephant early warning system ha been installed in 2 villages in the Kurunegala District and is reportedly working well. Fourth, a technical guide on construction and maintenance of electric fences. Fifth, a HECOEX study for the HKK Cluster in the dry zone.  In addition, two publications in peer reviewed scientific journals have been produced. Updating the National Master Plan was originally part of planned project activities, but the activity was dropped in June 2020 (during the partial credit cancellation) and covered by the GoSL itself. The knowledge generated is helping to inform elephant management in response to the human-elephant conflict in Sri Lanka and will feed into the next update of the National Master Plan. Data sources: various reports.</p>

<p><strong>Achieved (100%)</strong>. The indicator tracks the number of CAPs prepared by FD and DWC, respectively, and follows the pathway of <strong>wide use of improved livelihood activities</strong>. At closing, a total of 60 CAPs had been prepared to identify community needs in a participatory process for rural communities living near PAs. The result includes 47 CAPs prepared by FD and 13 CAPs prepared by DWC with livelihood and infrastructure activities targeting families in the buffer zones of participating PAs (see Annex 9 for an overview of activities by project areas). CAPs were developed in consultation with selected communities, journalists environmentalists, politicians and other community leaders over the design and proposals of livelihood activities in environmentally sensitive areas activities. Activities focused on a range of alternative livelihood options with income-generating potential related to agriculture and livestock-farming, off-farm activities, and community development programs (see Annex 1.B for an overview). Data sources: CAPs.</p>

title.narrative: Protected Area level nature-based tourism plans

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (100%). </strong>The indicator tracks the number of nature-based tourism plans developed at the level of PAs and thus relates to the pathway of <strong>improved tourism experience</strong>. A target of seven NBT plans was set and included three for DWC (Bundala, Udawalawe, and Yala) and four for FD (Hurulu, Kanneliya, Knuckles, and Sinharaja). At project closing, all NBT plans have been finalized. For Yala, the existing NBT plan was reviewed and updated but not publicly disclosed. In a decision by the Cabinet of August 28, 2023 the plans have been recommended for implementation to help rebuild the economy. Data sources: NBT plans (www.escamp.lk).</p>

title.narrative: People with improved access to income generating activities as a result of project interventions

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Partially Achieved (68%). </strong>The project sought to improve access to improved alternative IGA to reduce pressure on natural resources inside PAs, i.e. to reduce livelihood dependency on PAs. The indicator is linked to pathway of <strong>wide use of improved livelihood activities</strong>. The target was defined based on the number of beneficiaries identified in the CAPSs (see intermediate indicator 2). At project completion, the final Community Beneficiary Survey showed that 21,803 people participated inncome-generating and nature-based tourism activities realized on the basis of 60 CAPs (comp. 2.A and 3.B combined) and has been corrected for double counting.  Livelihood activities fell into three categories of support. First, agriculture-related activities, such as aloe vera, cinnamon, ginger, pepper, mushroom, and tea cultivation, home gardening, bee keeping, floriculture, kittul production, and nursery management. Second, livestock-related activities, such as goat keeping, poultry farming, and dairy production. Third, nature-based tourism and other off-farm activities, such as homestays, dress-making, food processing, tour guiding, and other small business (see Annex 9<strong> </strong>for an overview of IGA and their beneficiaries). The final CBS finds that 69% of participants report that they benefitted from “improved access to income-generating activities as a result of project interventions”. Beyond the CAPs, opportunities for providing manual labor for i.e. removal of invasive species have helped create additional income in local communities while supporting conservation outcomes. Data source: Community Beneficiary Survey (www.escamp.lk).</p>

title.narrative: Institutional framework for sustainable management of the fencing program in place

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (100%).</strong> The project has achieved institutionalization to ensure sustainable management of the fencing program which related to the pathway of <strong>reduced likelihood and severity of HEC</strong>. First, a formal agreement was reached in February 2023 with MoPAs that community-based permanent village fences will be institutionalized within the two participating Divisional Secretariats (DSs) (Kurunegala and Anuradhapura). This agreement obligates the DSs to undertake implementation, facilitation and monitoring of the permanent village fences. Awareness training of Divisional Secretariats and a Training-of-Trainers program is scheduled to take place in fall of 2023. Second, a formal agreement was reached with the Department of Agrarian Development (DAD to institutionalize the paddy-fences within the DAD. This obligates the DAD to erect the seasonal paddy-fences with the respective farmer organizations once all material is acquired.  Data sources: signed agreements.</p>

title.narrative: Trained staff demonstrating improved capacity for ecosystem management (index)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (100%).</strong> The indicator measures the demonstrated improved capacity of FD and DWC staff from training supported by the project on various dimensions of ecosystem management (see Annex 10) and pertains to the pathway of <strong>strengthened management capacity</strong>. By project closing, a total of 835 FD staff members had received training at the Sri Lanka Forestry Institute and 74 staff members from DWC had received training at the National Wildlife Research and Training Centre (see Annex 10). The result is assessed in a two-part survey, administered in August 2022, which invited staff members and their supervisors to evaluate training delivered between 2017 and 2022. The questionnaire was administered to the trainees and their immediate supervisors with a different set of questions for each group of respondents. Questions were perception-based and related to quality and content of the training (trainees) and improvement in work performance (supervisors). Rating scale: 1 = Very Low,  2 = Low,  3 = Medium, 4 = High, and 5 = Very High. Improved capacity was achieved if at least 50 percent of the respondents (simple average) rated the training as ‘Satisfactory’. The results are 87 percent for FD and 52 percent for DWC, and the overall target of ‘2’ was achieved. A total of 61 staff members from FD and 23 staff members from DWC participated in the survey, i.e. a low participation rate of 7 percent and 31 percent, respectively. Survey participation was voluntary but not anonymous. Data source: Capacity building survey and database.</p>

title.narrative: Strategically planned pilot landscapes with citizen participation

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (150%). </strong>The project piloted the development of two landscape management plans (LMP) in two different ecologically important zones, and on that basis prepared an Integrated Landscape Management Policy (ILMP). The indicator follows the pathway of a <strong>strong landscape planning framework</strong>. The documents were adopted by the National Planning Department (NPD) in May 2023 and have been submitted to the Cabinet for approval. The LMPs were developed with citizen participation in an inclusive process involving a national workshop in 2017, district-level workshops in 2020, and stakeholder consultations and dissemination workshops in 2018 to 2022 (delayed because of the pandemic). The need for an Integrated Landscape Management Policy arose from theack of institutional mechanisms to implement cross-sectoral ecosystem management using a landscape approach. If approved by the Cabinet, the ILMP will enter above other sector policies, such as infrastructure, environment, forest, and agriculture policies, to pilot integrated landscape-level management planning that enables more effective conservation of Sri Lanka’s unique landscapes and biologically diverse zones while promoting sustainable socio-economic development. Data sources: IMPs, ILMP (www.escamp.lk).</p>

title.narrative: Areas brought under enhanced biodiversity protection (ha)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (141%). </strong>The indicator relates to the pathways of <strong>improved PA management for carrying capacity and protection of wildlife</strong>. This is a proxy indicator that measures biodiversity protection as a result of the World Bank operation through formally converting an area into a protected area and establishing a functioning management system or improving the management system of an existing protected area. It is assessed using the Management Effectiveness Tracking Tool (METT) for Protectd Areas. At appraisal, the areas included in the target of 200,000 ha were not identified. When the target was revised upwards to 350,000 ha, it was defined based on the actual PAs that would benefit from project investments with a combined area of 363,648 ha (see Annex 9). At project closing, a total of 493,675 ha were benefitting from enhanced biodiversity protection through investments to strengthen PA management. First, 315,799 ha were benefitting from activities aimed at reducing forest and habitat degradation including demarcation of PA boundaries to protect against encroachment on 212,000 ha. Second, the project improved facilities used by forest rangers to patrol PAs covering an area of 393,116 ha, of which 215,240 ha are inside participating PAs (see Annex 9). At such, an additional 177,876 ha outside participating PAs are benefitting from improved biodiversity protection through rehabilitation and/or establishment of beat offices to strengthen the presence of forest rangers (see Annex 9). Combined, a total area of 493,675 ha are better protected against threats to biodiversity. METT assessments were not undertaken at project completion. Data sources: patrol logbooks, expert views, direct observation.</p>

title.narrative: Beneficiaries that agree project investments reflected their needs

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (103%). </strong>The indicator measures the perception of beneficiaries that project support for livelihood activities, community development, and HEC mitigation activities reflected the needs and priorities of communities. It is a corporately required indicator on citizen engagement, but it is not an outcome indicator and therefore not directly related to a pathway to the improved management of ecosystem management. At completion, the Community Beneficiary Survey shows that 77 percent of beneficiaries report that the project has responded satisfactorily to their needs by delivering benefits through livelihood and HECOEX activities Data source: Community Beneficiary Survey (www.escamp.lk).</p>

title.narrative: Visitors agree that investments and visitor management improvements have enhanced the quality of nature-based tourism

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved (170%). </strong>The indicator is linked to the pathway of <strong>improved tourism experience</strong>. At appraisal, the “Visitor revenue of selected PAs increased as a result of project interventions” with a target of 10 percent was included. It was revised due to difficulties in isolating externalities influencing PAs revenue from the attribution of project activities. The revised indicator measures the experience by recurring visitors of improved quality of tourism facilities in proteced areas supported by ESCAMP. The assessment is based on a Tourism Survey (itemized by sites with completed tourism infrastructure), which was administered to national tourists, who made repeat visits to the protected areas during the health crisis (foreign tourists tend to be one-time visitors and have only recently been able to visit SL again following the lock-down). The survey found that 85 percent of returning visitors have noticed an improvement in the quality of NBT facilities. The survey was undertaken in 2022 and did not include the visitor centers at Patanangala and Sinharaja as the site was still under construction. Data source: Beneficiary Response Survey of Local Tourists 2022.  </p>
